title: Ask forgiveness, and it rains
hookLine: ask forgiveness, He'll send rain, wealth, children and gardens (71:10–12)

lines: DAY AND NIGHT, IN PUBLIC AND IN PRIVATE.
cards: One man spends years trying to reach his own neighbors. He speaks quietly, one on one. He speaks in public.

He tries day and night. And they put their fingers in their ears and pull their clothes over their heads so they don't have to see him. That's how surah seventy-one, Nuh, describes Noah's preaching, in his own words.
And in the middle of it, he tells us exactly what he offered them. It wasn't a threat. It was rain.

teach.b: Surah Nuh is almost entirely Nuh speaking to his Lord, reporting how his people answered him. In verses ten to twelve, he tells what he said to them: ask forgiveness of your Lord, for He is ever forgiving.
He will send the sky down on you in abundant rain, give you more wealth and children, and give you gardens and rivers. Look at that chain.
Istighfar, asking forgiveness, comes first. What follows isn't only peace of mind. It's rain, money, family, green land, running water: things you can see from a window.
For people living by farming, rain was life. There's a story told in the commentaries about the early scholar al-Hasan al-Basri.
One man came to him complaining of drought, another of poverty, another of having no children, another of a dry garden.
To each he gave the same answer: ask Allah's forgiveness. When someone asked why, he recited these verses. Muslims also pray a special prayer for rain, salat al-istisqa', and istighfar is part of it.

And the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself, according to a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, asked Allah's forgiveness more than seventy times a day. Why would forgiveness open the sky? Commentators answer in different ways.
One picture: wrongdoing blocks things, and turning back clears the channel, less like paying a fee than like unclogging a pipe. The verses don't promise a deal on your schedule.
They describe a Lord who is ever forgiving, and generous after.

how: Muslims say astaghfirullah through the day, some in sets counted on fingers or prayer beads; istighfar is part of the prayer for rain (salat al-istisqa'), and 71:10–12 is recalled in times of drought and hardship.

o: a public apology made in front of the mosque
istighfar, asking forgiveness of your Lord
a prayer asking God for rain to fall

s: Nuh promised his people only punishment
in 71:10–12 he offered rain, wealth, children, gardens and rivers.
a hadith says the Prophet asked forgiveness over seventy times a day
the al-Hasan al-Basri story is in the Qur'an
it's a story told in the commentaries; the verses are its source.

games.q: you're al-Hasan al-Basri. four people come: drought, poverty, no children, a dry garden. what do you tell them?
games.why: the story says he gave each the same answer, and recited 71:10–12 when asked why.

practice: If you pray, say astaghfirullah softly, I ask Allah's forgiveness, counting on your fingers or on beads; you may get near a hundred or not, and any number is fine.
If you don't pray, count slow breaths instead, and on each out-breath let go of one small thing you're carrying against yourself or someone else.

wordCard.voice: Ask forgiveness. Istighfar. In 71:10–12 Nuh tells his people that asking forgiveness brings rain, wealth, children, gardens and rivers. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: I ask Allah's forgiveness. from the root gh-f-r, to cover, to forgive.

carryVoice: Your line: forgiveness brings rain. Turning back comes first, and the generosity follows. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 6307 (seeking forgiveness more than seventy times a day)
story of al-Hasan al-Basri and the four complaints, in tafsir on 71:10–12 (e.g. al-Qurtubi)
